rule: adjusted_score desc, total_score desc; dedupe by arXiv id / URL / id / title

papers.title: ReSID: Rethinking Long-Tail Retrieval in Generative Recommendation through Item Reachability
papers.authors: Muyu Zou, Shunye Tang, Yi Xu, Haibo Xing, Yandong Wang, Lingyu Mu, Jinxin Hu
papers.summary: Generative recommendation encodes each item as a string of Semantic ID tokens and generates them one position at a time with beam search, and cold long-tail items are hard to retrieve this way. The authors take apart the whole chain from encoding through decoding to matching and find that tail items are mostly lost early in decoding: on Amazon Industrial, 62.5% of tail targets have already fallen out of the beam after just two tokens. They also find that parallel SIDs, which split the vector into segments and quantize each separately, treat the tail better than sequential SIDs that quantize residuals layer by layer. The reason is that an error at one position does not spill into later ones, so a partly wrong sequence still keeps useful positions. ReSID therefore damps popularity bias and adds a user-semantic score inside beam search so tail prefixes survive, then allows a match even when some positions disagree. It now serves main traffic, raising ad revenue by 1.3% and the long-tail exposure share by 4.0%. ==Tail items are often pruned during decoding, and looser matching afterwards cannot bring them back==.

papers.title: TriGen: A Generative Paradigm for Trigger-Induced Recommendation
papers.authors: Muyu Zou, Haibo Xing, Shunye Tang, Liyan Tie, Lingyu Mu, Yandong Wang, Jinxin Hu
papers.summary: E-commerce has a common kind of recommendation: a user clicks an item in the main feed and lands at once in a feed built around that item. The recommendations must follow the intent of that click without throwing away the user's long-term taste. Generative recommendation by default just continues the user's history with more SIDs, so one click is easily diluted in a long history, while traditional methods rely on discriminative scoring and cannot steer token-by-token generation. Alibaba International's TriGen appends several copies of the clicked item to the end of the history so it mainly reshapes recent behavior. It then uses a gate to decide per request whether to follow the click or the history more, and keeps injecting the click signal at every decoding position. In online experiments in six Southeast Asian countries, revenue rose 3.27% and GMV 0.90%, and it is now fully deployed. ==In click-triggered feeds, the hard part is how much the click should override history, and that changes every time==.

papers.title: From Tokens to Behaviors: Rethinking Generative Recommendation for User Trajectory Prediction
papers.authors: Jiaqi Wang, Hanchen Yang, Hengyu Zhang, Hongxu Ma, Wenqi Rao, Hongyang Wang, Zhongbo Sun, Renliang Qian, Weixin Chen, We...
papers.summary: Most recommenders guess only the user's next click, while user trajectory prediction guesses the next several steps at once, such as buying running shoes and then sports socks and a water bottle. Generative recommendation does this by generating each item's SID token by token before moving to the next item, so the encoding within an item and the transitions between items are tangled in one chain. Worse, each step passes on only the chosen item: if the model gives socks 50% and running shoes 35%, later steps see only the socks and the shoe clue is lost. TraGR generates all SID positions of an item in parallel, moves between items with a recurrent state, passes on the chosen item plus a probability-weighted summary of the other candidates, and trains on trajectories the model generates itself. On four public datasets it beats the strongest baselines, and its lead holds at longer horizons. ==In trajectory prediction, candidates not chosen at one step are useful clues for the steps after it==.

papers.title: SimRec: Learning to Search, Ask, and Recommend from Simulated Interaction
papers.authors: Yaxin Zhang, Xingyu Wu, Yuchen Yan, Yuqin Dai, Hong Zhao, Lixing Shen, Zhan Chen, Jian Shao, Yongliang Shen
papers.summary: LLM-based recommendation agents can search a catalog, open product details, ask the user, and try another item after a rejection, but when to search, ask, or recommend is mostly a hand-written workflow. Existing training only practices single steps such as rewriting a query or ranking a list, so the outcome of the whole conversation never reaches the policy making those decisions. The authors find that such agents seldom check the candidates they retrieve, seldom consult the user's history, and rarely recover after a rejection, and a bigger model does not make up for it. SimRec trains the whole interaction with reinforcement learning: a simulated user who knows the task need but not the target item gives feedback on every recommendation, and the reward counts retrieval quality, valid tool use, and the final hit. On ESCI it lifts the NDCG@100 of a Qwen3-4B agent from 32.23% to 35.42%, beating untrained agents on much larger backbones. ==What recommendation agents lack is checking candidates and recovering after a rejection, and a bigger model does not supply it==.

papers.title: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence
papers.authors: Pan Li, Alexander Tuzhilin
papers.summary: Recommenders are often asked to break users out of filter bubbles, yet a user's curiosity has never had a definition a system can compute. Existing proxies such as unexpectedness and variety-seeking only look at how far an item sits from the user's taste. Picture two videos equally far from that taste: the user has watched many items similar to the first and none similar to the second. Distance scores them the same, but curiosity needs partial knowledge, so only the first makes the user aware of something missing. The authors turn the information-gap theory from psychology into five axioms and derive a curiosity score computed from consumption records alone, which matches self-reported curiosity in a survey. With this score added to the ranking objective next to relevance, an online experiment on a large Asian video platform raised click-through by 2.75 percentage points and watch time by 0.71 minutes per recommendation, and the method is now deployed. ==Curiosity depends on how much the user already knows, and distance alone cannot measure it==.

papers.title: Serving-Aligned Entire-Space Conversion Modeling via Click-Through Rate Knowledge Distillation
papers.authors: Pavel Dolin, Xun Zou, Jiatian Wu, Deguang Kong
papers.summary: Ranking often multiplies a click-through prediction by a conversion prediction to get the probability of a click followed by a purchase. Many conversion models are trained with ESMM, which carries its own auxiliary click-through tower trained together with the conversion tower, but only the conversion tower is deployed and multiplied by a separately trained production click-through model. The trouble is that the conversion tower was trained alongside the auxiliary tower's click rates, while in serving it is multiplied by the production model's click rates, so the product drifts when the two disagree. The Reddit authors leave the production click-through model alone and distill ESMM's auxiliary tower from the production click-through scores already stored in the logs, so the tower matches the production model during training. On Ali-CCP, the best setting raises PR-AUC of the product actually used in serving by 9.9%, and the conversion tower itself improves too. The gain survives when only 5% of negatives are kept. ==In joint multi-tower training, the auxiliary tower should learn the model it is actually paired with in serving==.

papers.title: Measuring, Revealing and Mitigating Harmful Content Propagation in Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Xiaokun Zhang, Youlin Wu, Junyu Lu, Jiamin Chen, Zhaochun Ren, Hongfei Lin, Fenglong Ma, Xue Liu, Chen Ma
papers.summary: Recommenders chase user interest, and few ask whether what they push is harmful. The authors sampled 100 recommendation lists produced by BERT4Rec and found that nearly half of the items contained gender discrimination, misinformation, or offensive language. They had an LLM label the items in three news and advertising datasets as harmful or healthy with a reason, then had humans review the labels. The data shows that more than half of the content in each dataset is labeled harmful, and harmful items get more interactions on average than healthy ones. Mainstream recommendation models learn from those interactions, and their lists are mostly less than half healthy. Their MitiHarm adds harmfulness signals to both item and user representations, and on the QB dataset it raises the share of healthy items in NARM's top 5 by 54.01% while largely keeping accuracy. ==Users click harmful content more, so a model trained only on interactions pushes more of it==.

papers.title: Sheaf-Inspired Structured Scoring Extensions of LightGCN for Collaborative Filtering
papers.authors: Ksenia Belkovskaya, Timur Lidzhiev, Maria Stebliy, Alexander Tarakanov
papers.summary: In graph collaborative filtering, after embeddings are propagated over the user-item graph, LightGCN's final step scores a pair with a plain inner product. Borrowing the idea of a sheaf from mathematics, the authors keep the propagation and change only the scorer, so that user and item embeddings pass through a linear transformation that depends on the pair before being compared. They try diagonal, rank-one, and full-matrix transformations, with a parameter-matched MLP scorer as the control. On Amazon-Book, Gowalla, MovieLens-1M, and Yelp2018, the selected structured scorers edge out both the inner product and the MLP on NDCG@20, for example from 0.031028 to 0.031302 on Amazon-Book, a very small gap. The MLP often covers more of the catalog. The authors state the caveats plainly: the candidates were picked after the fact from test results, Amazon-Book has only one seed, and no actual sheaf is built, so the gains cannot be credited to sheaf geometry. The paper is best read as an honest negative reference.

papers.title: KuaiRecV2: Benchmarking Large-Scale Continual Learning for Diversified and Multi-task Recommendation
papers.authors: Chenxu Li, Shuchang Liu, Hantao Shu, Wei Yuan, Zhe Xu, Guoqing Hu, Yan Wang, Biao Yang, Xiang Li, Cheng Ling, Fan Yang, ...
papers.summary: One reason recommenders look good offline and disappoint online is that offline data is too static: the candidate pool never changes, and diversity and multiple behaviors go unscored. Kuaishou's KuaiRecV2 puts these factors into one benchmark built from real data. It holds 30 days of behavior from 124 thousand users, the candidate video pool is updated first-in, first-out every day, and models must keep training day by day as they would in production. Evaluation looks at retrieval accuracy, diversity, and several behaviors such as likes and long views together, and a method counts as an advance only if every metric improves. Running several generative recommenders on it, the authors find that models forget old knowledge and that the SIDs generated under the same prefix are nearly identical. More counterintuitively, an RL-only model does improve on day 20 but drops sharply on day 21 once the pool changes, and only alternating with SFT keeps it stable. ==Aligning multiple behaviors with RL alone is fragile when the candidate pool shifts==.

papers.title: Too much of a good thing: Why 20 candidates beat 200 when reranking search results
papers.authors: Scott Martens, Sofia Vasileva
papers.summary: Is it always better to give a reranker more candidates? Jina's team at Elastic tested its own listwise reranker on more than two dozen retrieval benchmarks, and the answer is no. With BM25 as the first stage, reranking the top 100 candidates works best, cutting about a fifth of the error on average, and adding more makes it worse. With semantic search as the first stage, the best point moves down to 20 candidates and the gain is much smaller, and sending 200 is on average worse than not reranking at all. The reason is that a listwise model reads the whole candidate list at once, so with too many candidates its attention is spread thin and noise accumulates. A model that scores candidates one by one does not have this problem, since an extra candidate never changes the order of the others. The worse the first stage, the more candidates reranking needs and the more room it has to fix things. ==Size the candidate pool by the quality of the first stage, because sending too many hurts==

papers.title: AntEmbed: Dual-Mode Multimodal Embedding Model for Efficient and Fine-Grained Retrieval
papers.authors: Kehang Jia, Teng Liu, Juntao Li, Hua Chen, Jinxiong Chang, Xiaobo Liang, Min Zhang
papers.summary: Multimodal retrieval has two kinds of embeddings. Discriminative embeddings encode the raw input directly, which is fast but misses fine-grained meaning. Generative embeddings first have the model reason about the query intent and distinguishing evidence and then encode, which is more accurate but adds a reasoning pass to every query. AntEmbed, from Soochow University and Ant Group, lets one model do both while sharing a single candidate index. It treats the raw input and the input with reasoning added as two views of the same thing and pulls them into one vector space with multi-positive contrastive learning. It then distills the candidate similarity distribution from the reasoning view into the raw representation so that the non-reasoning mode gets stronger too. On MMEB-v2, AntEmbed-8B scores 81.5 overall in reasoning mode, 3.1 points above the strongest baseline. The 2B model scores 70.2 even without reasoning, beating several generative models that do reason. ==One index can choose per query between reasoning and direct retrieval==

papers.title: CURATOR: Scalable Fine-grained Evidence Selection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Decision Models
papers.authors: Shib Dasgupta, Bandish Parikh, Rashmi Gangadharaiah
papers.summary: RAG usually stuffs whole retrieved passages into the LLM, though often only a few sentences in them can answer the question. Picking those sentences is not easy: a sentence can look irrelevant on its own, and whether to keep it may depend on other retrieved text. Judging each sentence with the full context is too expensive. Decision models can score many candidate sentences in one pass, with each judgment seeing the surrounding sentences. But the authors find that the more judgments they must make at once, the worse they get at telling useful evidence apart, and one retrieval step often brings hundreds of candidates. CURATOR trains a decision model specifically to pick a variable number of supporting sentences from a large pool while keeping the efficiency of scoring in one pass. Under a 128-token context budget, it raises evidence recall by 17.0% on average on unseen datasets and domains, and downstream answer quality by 17.4%. ==The tighter the context, the more it matters to pick the right evidence rather than add more passages==

papers.title: UMER: Unifying Embedding and Ranking via Pair-Aware Discriminative Reasoning for Universal Multimodal Retrieval
papers.authors: Libiao Chen, Xiyang Liu, Yanheng Wei, Zhenyu Tang
papers.summary: When multimodal LLMs are used for embeddings, a recent trend is to have the model write a chain of thought before encoding, injecting intermediate semantic evidence into the representation. The problem is that these chains are written for the query and the candidate separately, never seeing the hard negative that looks like the positive, so they cannot say why the positive is right or where the hard negative falls short. UMER switches to pairwise reasoning: it puts the query and candidate side by side and writes the evidence that matches the instruction and the evidence that does not. One MLLM learns both an embedding that can be indexed alone for full-corpus retrieval and a pairwise relevance judgment, and the two then distill reliable preferences into each other. In serving one can retrieve with the embedding alone and turn on pairwise reranking when the budget allows. On MMEB-V2, UMER with a Qwen2-VL-7B backbone scores 70.6, 2.0 points above the strongest baseline on the same backbone. ==To tell positives from hard negatives, reasoning has to compare them side by side==

papers.title: Calibration and Conformal Prediction for Medical Question Answering in Arabic and English: Evidence from Two Non-Parallel Benchmarks
papers.authors: Mariya
papers.summary: An LLM's accuracy on medical exam questions cannot say which individual answer can be trusted. The author takes two 7B open models and checks whether their option probabilities are reliable on English MedMCQA and Arabic MedAraBench multiple-choice questions. In all four combinations the raw probabilities are overconfident, and a single temperature parameter removes more than 80% of the calibration error. Conformal prediction reaches its promised coverage in every setting, but the answer sets are large when accuracy is low: to guarantee 90% coverage, Jais's sets on Arabic questions contain 89% of the options on average. Answering only the most confident fifth of questions cuts Qwen's English error from 0.439 to 0.098. The two benchmarks differ in subject and difficulty, so the author does not attribute the differences to language itself. ==When a model is not accurate enough, a coverage guarantee alone cannot yield useful answer sets==

papers.title: Authenticated Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in Outsourced Vector Databases
papers.authors: Yuanhang Zhou, Xinyi Zhang, Cheng Xu, Jianliang Xu
papers.summary: Once a vector database is outsourced to a third-party cloud, the provider may skip neighbors to save compute or even tamper with results, so the client needs a way to verify that a nearest-neighbor search is genuine. Existing methods have the cloud send back the traversal path on the graph index along with every raw vector visited on the way, and the client recomputes the distances itself. Embeddings often have thousands of dimensions, so this proof becomes enormous. VIDA sends vector commitments instead, whose size does not depend on the dimension, and uses one aggregated inner product proof to verify many distance computations at once. A matching authentication structure makes the proof paths follow the graph traversal, and distance bounds from quantization prune a batch of points that then need no cryptographic check. Against the best existing methods, end-to-end latency is up to 6.6 times faster and data transfer time drops by up to 99.2%. ==Most of the verification cost is shipping raw high-dimensional vectors, and commitments remove most of it==.

papers.title: Benchmarking tiered KV cache offloading on H100 GPUs in OpenShift AI 3.5
papers.authors: Ramesh Doddaiah, Alberto Perdomo, Nathan Scott, Ashish Kamra, Michey Mehta, Yuchen Fama, Naina Singh
papers.summary: Long-context agent requests resend the same prefix again and again, so the KV cache could be reused, but once GPU memory fills up it is thrown away and recomputed next time. Red Hat offloads the KV cache in OpenShift AI 3.5 to CPU memory, local NVMe, or shared CephFS, and gives a rule for judging a tier: it is worth using only when its p99 restore latency is below the prefill time a cache hit saves. On agent workloads averaging about 50 thousand input tokens, Nemotron-Ultra-253B throughput rose by up to 5.8 times. The difference depends on whether the working set fits in the CPU tier. When it does not, offloading to CPU memory alone gives only 3.3 times, and adding NVMe or CephFS nearly doubles that. When it fits, the CPU tier alone captures most of the gain. With multiple replicas under high concurrency, shared CephFS lets replicas reuse the same cache. ==Size the working set first, then decide whether a second storage tier is needed==

papers.title: SoScale: Second-Order Scale Search for FP4 Quantization
papers.authors: Pengxiang Zhao, Xing Li, Hui-Ling Zhen, Weizhe Lin, Xianzhi Yu, Zhenhua Dong
papers.summary: In FP4 quantization each number has only 16 possible values, and each block of data gets one scale that decides where those grid points land. The default scales by the block's maximum absolute value, so outliers stretch the grid. In a real Qwen3-8B weight block, the authors find that the two outermost grid points receive no values at all, while the dense majority of values near zero get too little resolution. Existing scale searches pick scales by element-wise reconstruction error, judging whether the weights look right rather than whether the layer's output does. SoScale searches only among hardware-valid scale codes, picks them by Hessian-weighted layer output error, and alternates this with GPTQ-style error compensation so later blocks absorb the error of earlier ones. On two Qwen3 models and three FP4 formats it has the best average score in every group, and Qwen3-14B under MXFP4 keeps 97.17% of BF16 average accuracy. ==Scales should be chosen by layer output, since weight error alone picks them poorly==

papers.title: VecDBLens: An Evaluatology-Based Framework for Vector Database Diagnosis
papers.authors: Yutong Zhou, Guoxin Kang, Wenxin Zhou, Haoyu He, Yuedong Zhu, Lei Wang, Wanling Gao, Fanda Fan, Jianfeng Zhan
papers.summary: When a vector database recalls poorly, the first instinct is to tune the index, but the ceiling on what an index can find is set by the embedding. On VisualNews with SigLIP2 and exact brute-force search, the authors find that only 2.04% of the nearest images by distance are the paired image in the labels. By contrast, graph indexes such as HNSW and CAGRA keep almost all of exact search's recall. When the candidate pool grows, Qwen3-VL keeps 72.3% of its recall on average while SigLIP2 keeps only 33.2%. VecDBLens changes one object at a time, such as the embedding model, the index, or query processing, holds all data, workloads, and parameters fixed, and then uses analysis of variance to see how they interact. It also finds that overly aggressive index parameters reshape neighborhoods and lower recall for filtered queries. ==When recall stalls, check the embedding first, because many apparent index problems come from the representation==

papers.title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
papers.authors: Yong Li, Haoyu Wang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
papers.summary: Expert-parallel MoE decoding is latency bound: every layer must dispatch tokens to the GPUs, run grouped matrix multiplies over the experts, and combine the results, three steps in series, with very few tokens in flight on each GPU. The earlier GC-MoE fused the three steps into one persistent CUDA Graph on Hopper and datacenter Blackwell. This paper moves it to consumer Blackwell cards over PCIe, such as the RTX PRO 5000. These cards expose block-scaled matrix multiplies only through warp-level instructions and lack several hardware features of datacenter parts, so the original kernel cannot be used directly. The authors rewrite the whole operator around a warp-level multiply of FP4 weights by FP8 activations and redo the per-expert streaming dispatch and the return path. On eight RTX PRO 5000 cards it is on average 1.522 times faster than FlashInfer's comparable operator, wins all 18 decode test points, and passes every numerical check. ==The same fusion idea had to be almost rewritten from scratch for consumer hardware==

papers.title: Snoopie: A Multi-GPU Communication Profiler and Visualizer
papers.authors: Mohammad Kefah Taha Issa, Muhammad Aditya Sasongko, Ilyas Turimbetov, Javid Baydamirli, Doğan Sağbili, Didem Unat
papers.summary: Multi-GPU programs often fail to scale because of data movement, yet existing tools cannot show clearly who moves what. NVIDIA's Nsight Systems only hints that there is traffic on NVLink, without showing which GPU issued a direct memory access or which object it touched, and it cannot show what actually moves beneath NCCL and NVSHMEM calls. Snoopie uses binary instrumentation on NVBit to track peer-to-peer transfers and communication library calls, maps every transfer to a source line and data object, and can zoom from the whole system down to single instructions and addresses. In one case study, a BFS program with ring communication showed unexpected traffic between GPU 1 and GPU 3, and the object view pointed to a flag pointer array allocated only on GPU 3, and fixing the allocation removed the extra transfers. The cost is heavy instrumentation overhead, especially on the NCCL case. ==It suits tracking down communication problems, not running permanently in production==

papers.title: SubGPU Pipelining: Intra-GPU Fine-Grained Spatial Parallelism for LLM Inference
papers.authors: Muralidhar Andoorveedu, Marius Juston, Tingkai Liu, Sanjay Patel
papers.summary: LLM decode is a string of very short kernels, most of them limited by memory bandwidth. Running them one after another, each with the whole GPU, leaves compute and bandwidth alternately idle and busy, and many SMs sit unused while bandwidth is saturated. SubGPU Pipelining builds a pipeline inside one GPU. It cuts the operator graph into contiguous segments, binds each segment to its own disjoint group of SMs, and splits a batch into small batches that stream through in order, so work with complementary needs runs at the same time. Where to cut, how many SMs each segment gets, and how big the small batches are all affect one another, and the authors search them with a simulator that models shared-resource contention. In a simulated GPT-OSS 120B deployment on 32 B200s, at equal per-GPU throughput the per-user throughput is up to 2.2 times higher. Hardware tests validated only one two-segment configuration on a single B200, cutting decoder iteration time by 10.33%. ==A pipeline inside one GPU can stagger and fill resources that would otherwise sit idle in turns==

papers.title: Towards Green Text Generation: Memory-Based Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Antal van den Bosch
papers.summary: Speculative decoding has a cheap draft model guess a few tokens, which a large model then checks in one forward pass. Once the verifier uses a KV cache it is already much faster, so the cost of the draft model can no longer be ignored. On consumer hardware the authors find that a TinyLlama draft has a high acceptance rate yet halves throughput and triples energy. Their Olifant draft is not a neural network at all but a memory-based classification tree that predicts the next token from the previous four, returns in under 0.3 ms on CPU, and needs no GPU and no backpropagation. With a KV-cached verifier it still delivers 1.25 times the throughput and the lowest energy in the whole study. They also find that the KV cache decouples speed from energy: longer drafts raise power draw during verification, so the most energy-efficient draft length is shorter than the fastest one. ==The faster the verifier, the closer to free the draft must be==

papers.title: When One GPU Isn’t Enough: Serving GLM-5.3 Across Two NVIDIA DGX Stations with vLLM
papers.authors: Fatima Fall
papers.summary: The NVFP4 version of GLM-5.3 is a large MoE model in which each token activates only a small share of the parameters, but each token may be routed to different experts, so all weights must stay in GPU memory. The full weights are about 464 GB, and a single GB300 has only 252 GB of memory, so they do not fit. This NVIDIA tutorial links two DGX Stations directly over RDMA, splits weights and compute in half with tensor parallelism, serves one OpenAI-compatible endpoint through vLLM, and turns on multi-token prediction, an FP8 KV cache, and prefix caching. Under a coding benchmark, total throughput peaks at concurrency 16 and falls at concurrency 32, where mean request latency stretches to seven and a half minutes and each user gets slower and slower. ==When running a huge model locally, more concurrency is not always better, so benchmark first to find the turning point==

papers.title: How to Use AI Coding in a System That Must Not Fail: Practice and Limits in Distributed Storage
papers.summary: Meituan's distributed storage team shares what it learned using AI to write code in a system that must not fail. They start with a simple calculation: even if AI code has the same defects per thousand lines as human code, shipping more code means more defects in absolute terms. AI review is good at finding inconsistencies across files and will even build malformed inputs to reproduce a crash, but it cannot see what lies outside the code, such as manual operations or deliberate designs like letting the process exit rather than writing dirty data. The team turned each of the 117 suspected issues from one full-repository review into a unit test. An issue counted as confirmed only if its test failed on the main branch, and 36 were confirmed, 3 were refuted, and the rest could only be confirmed by reading source or not verified yet. When they gave runtime logs to the AI to map back to source, every defect it found was confirmed by people. ==AI review only finds candidates, and tests and logs decide which are real==

papers.title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
papers.authors: Zhuoyue Li, Zhendong Han, Pankhuri Vanjani, Wenting Li, Rudolf Lioutikov
papers.summary: A VLA model predicts a short chunk of future actions at a time, and when objects move, that chunk goes stale before it finishes executing. The authors use a pretrained π0.5 on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. They systematically compare how far to predict, how many steps to execute each time, and synchronous or asynchronous inference. The best prediction length is about one second, asynchronous inference helps more when the execution horizon is short, and methods that keep successive trajectories continuous beat those that only reduce latency. The biggest surprise is the conveyor picking task. Fine-tuning the policy with reinforcement learning fixes targeted failures, but the same checkpoint with no training at all reaches 71% success just by setting the execution horizon to 5, as good as after training. ==How fast a robot reacts depends on how it executes as much as on the policy, so evaluate the two together==

papers.title: Scaling VLA Serving Under Robotic Execution Constraints
papers.authors: Yue Zhang, Zicong Ye, Lufang Chen, Dance Yang, Mingyang Li, Zhenwei Duan, Michael Zhao, Ziye Deng, Starrick Liu, Ruizhi ...
papers.summary: The authors' company already has hundreds of VLA-driven robots working in real environments, and robots must share GPUs to keep inference costs down. Robots keep executing old actions while waiting for new ones. So among requests of the same size, some robots are about to run out and need a reply now, while others can wait. Admitting one more request on the GPU also slows the requests already running, and once a robot's action queue empties it must stop and wait. XInfer breaks VLA computation into stages that proceed as soon as their dependencies are ready, and its scheduler uses each robot's current urgency to decide what to compute first and when a new request may join. On three VLA models with production-derived workloads, the number of robots one GPU can serve under real-time requirements is 1.26 to 3.75 times that of the best existing systems. ==When serving a robot fleet, a request's urgency depends on how many actions the robot has left==

papers.title: Learning Low-Latency Action Verification for Frozen Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Wen-Han Hsieh, Ken Jiankun Zheng, Chia-Chien Chen, David M. Chan, Trevor Darrell
papers.summary: The actions a VLA model samples are not always good, and sampling several and picking one is safer, but using a large model as the judge adds a long wait to every query. The authors' HDH trains its judge only on records from the frozen VLA's own deployments. The policy first runs a batch of tasks on its own and the final outcome after each action chunk is recorded. A small model then learns to predict, from the current view and the actions already executed, how likely a candidate chunk is to end in success. At deployment the VLA generates two candidates and the small model executes the higher-scoring one, with no expert labels and no predicted future frames. On four LIBERO-10 tasks, average success rises from 78.8% to 82.3% with only 5.4% more query latency, more accurate and faster than GPT-family judges, and the gain is larger on three real-robot tasks. ==A robot's own record of successes and failures is enough to teach a cheap action judge==

papers.title: ILA: A Transferable Interface-Level Adapter for Compliant Humanoid Motion Tracking
papers.authors: ZhuoChang Cai, Zihao Yan, Jinxuan Zhu, Yanjie Li, Hao Xiong
papers.summary: Humanoid robots that track human motion are often used for teleoperation and motion data collection. But following the reference motion rigidly is unsafe in tight spaces or when a person is in physical contact, and it struggles to yield when someone guides its arm. ILA leaves the original tracking policy unchanged and adds an adapter in front of it: from the robot's recent observation history, it infers where an external force is trying to move the motion and edits the reference handed to the tracker accordingly. The adapter is trained entirely in simulation and needs no dedicated force sensor. The same trained adapter plugs straight into three independently trained trackers with neither side retrained, cutting the error of guiding an arm to a target by 63.6% to 75.4% while largely keeping normal tracking. On hardware, none of the original trackers could be pulled to a lateral-raise target, while every tracker with the adapter reached it in all ten trials. ==Compliance can be a generic plug-in layer outside the tracking policy==

papers.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
papers.authors: Jiachun Jin, Zetong Zhou, Haonan Wang, Xiao Yang, Jun Zhu, Zhijie Deng
papers.summary: Robot interaction data is expensive, while first-person human video is cheap and plentiful, and a common approach uses latent action models to extract action signals from video to supervise policies. The problem is that most of these models learn only by reconstructing video, so their latent actions cluster by how the scene looks rather than by what action was taken, and human actions fail to line up with robot actions. SALA needs no paired human and robot data. It uses the text descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarity, pulls human latent actions toward semantically similar robot latents, and grounds the latent space in control through robot action reconstruction. Human video then helps in two directions. More general human video in pre-training keeps lowering the robot's action prediction error on downstream tasks. With teleoperation data fixed, adding human demonstrations of the target task in post-training raises average real-robot success from 53.75% to 72.5%. ==Latent actions must align by action meaning before human video can truly supervise robots==

papers.title: FORGE: Force-Aware Multi-Granularity Control for Efficient Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Liangjun Xing, Ke Fan, Kailin Li, Bin Wang, Xiaojie Niu, Qingwei Ben, Jiafei Cao, Wei Yao, Yebin Liu, Jingbo Wang, Weina...
papers.summary: Getting a humanoid robot to walk while carrying things makes teleoperated data collection hard: the controller must be precise, stay balanced, and know how much force its hands feel. FORGE gives the operator coarse-to-fine commands for walking speed, where the feet land, where the wrists go, and an optional desired force, usable alone or together. Training needs no human whole-body motion trajectories, and deployment needs only the two wrist poses relative to the pelvis plus rough movement commands. With no force sensor at the wrist, it estimates hand forces from joint states and low-level motor torques, adding a simulator-supervised learned correction on top of a momentum-based estimator. A frozen walking policy anchors the lower body, and a residual policy learns the upper body plus any needed lower-body corrections, which makes training more stable. A diffusion policy trained on top of it carries boxes from 0 to 2 kg on the real robot, 20 trials per load, with at least 18 successes even on the hardest one. ==Without wrist force sensors, motor torques can still give a usable force estimate==

papers.title: I See What You Want: Decoding Hierarchical Operator Intent from Visual Teleoperation History
papers.authors: Xiangyi Jia, Kaixian Qu, Shengzhi Wang, Chenyu Yang, Robert Katzschmann, Marco Hutter
papers.summary: When a person teleoperates a robot, can a large model tell what they want just from the video? The authors split this into two levels, the action happening now and the overall task it serves, and build a dataset of teleoperation episodes from many kinds of robots. Off-the-shelf large models do poorly here. VIM, fine-tuned on this data, raises the semantic similarity between predicted and true task descriptions from GPT-4o's 0.470 to 0.821. The more practical result is downstream: the task VIM infers is handed to a VLA policy that takes over midway and finishes the remaining manipulation, and in unseen real environments the human teleoperation time drops 34.6% compared with using GPT-4o to infer intent. ==Guessing the operator's intent correctly lets the robot take over midway==

papers.title: Adapt Human Motion for Robots with NVIDIA SOMA Retargeter
papers.authors: John Malaska
papers.summary: Human motion is a good starting point for teaching humanoid robots to move, but a robot's proportions, joint structure, and range of motion differ from a person's, so human joint angles cannot be copied directly. NVIDIA's open-source SOMA Retargeter handles this conversion. It first puts human motion from motion capture, video reconstruction, or generative models onto a shared SOMA skeleton. It then scales the targets to the robot's proportions and solves joint poses frame by frame with inverse kinematics. Finally it removes problems such as foot sliding while a foot is planted, so a downstream tracking policy does not receive conflicting targets. The post gives an example: for the same one-handed wave, a robot whose reference pose is not aligned with the human holds both arms out, and only after alignment does one hand wave while the other hangs down. The current release ships reference configurations for five humanoid robots, and its output trajectories convert directly into formats for training motion-tracking policies. ==Retargeting quality often hinges on details such as whether the reference poses are aligned==

papers.title: Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets
papers.authors: Dillon Bailey, Pomi Lee, Rishabh Chadha
papers.summary: In robot pick-and-place simulation, a robot can look correct while stationary and still move or touch objects incorrectly once the simulation runs. This NVIDIA tutorial builds a beverage-can pick example with the SimReady asset library on Hugging Face. SimReady means an asset already has the physical properties needed for a given simulation use, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. The tutorial places an arm, a gripper, and a can in Isaac Sim, then has an AI agent that can call Isaac Sim skills assemble the robot, check joints and contacts, and generate control code to grasp, lift, move, and release. The authors also state the limits: the can starts at a fixed position, no vision is used, collision checks are limited, and the can neither deforms nor simulates liquid, so the result says nothing about uncertain positions, other payloads, or real hardware. ==Assets with the right physical properties are only a start, and the assembled scene still has to be run to know==

papers.title: Six AGIBOT G2 Robots Complete 1,730 Tasks in 24-Hour Shanghai Convenience Store Trial
papers.summary: Six AGIBOT G2 wheeled humanoid robots staffed an operating convenience store in Shanghai's Xuhui District for 24 hours straight, handling customer assistance, shelf inspection and restocking, coffee, checkout and hot food, and cleaning, and completed 1,730 tasks in total. The whole trial was livestreamed, and evaluators set deliberate tests. They ordered regular and sugar-free Coca-Cola to see whether the robots could tell similar products apart. They rearranged chewing gum on a shelf to see whether it would be put back, and blocked an aisle with a person and a box to see whether they would go around. In the end four of the six robots passed the assessment and two did not meet every criterion. AGIBOT coordinated the six robots with its own agent framework, collecting the success or failure of each execution for analysis and turning effective adjustments into training data. This was a vendor-run showcase, and the report gives no details such as failure rates. ==In a real store, the hard part is coping with situations that differ slightly every time==
